title: How to Talk to AI
author: kristinjackvony
text: One of the great features of AI is that it allows you to use natural language when giving it instructions. That’s also one of the great drawbacks: when using language instead of code, you can create interactions with AI that are expensive, inefficient, and dangerous. Let’s look at five rules to use when interacting with an AI. Rule #1: The AI is not your friend You might be greeted with great enthusiasm by your AI when you first open it up in the morning, but that does not mean that the AI is your friend. The AI does not like you. The AI does not like anything , because the AI is a software program built upon vast amounts of data. So there is no reason to wish your AI a good morning, or say please and thank-you, or tell it that you are done working for the day. Not only do these expressions waste time, they waste money as well! Every character that you send the AI has a cost in tokens, and while little words like “please” might not cost much, repeated use of unnecessary words can really add up. I promise your AI will not be hurt if you don’t thank it! Rule #2: Check the information that the AI gives you As I mentioned in a previous post , the AI can be wrong. The AI only knows what it has been trained to know, and some of its training materials can be flawed. Consider for example the story of the Bereavement Fare on Air Canada . The Air Canada chatbot told passengers that they could apply for a bereavement fare after their trip, when in reality they were required to apply before the trip. A good rule of thumb when working with AI responses is: if it sounds wrong, it probably is wrong. Ask the AI where it got the information. Ask the AI how certain it is of its information. You can even ask another AI to verify the AI’s response! Rule #3: Give the AI specific instructions As mentioned above, interactions with AI cost tokens, which cost money. So it’s a good idea to keep your interactions as efficient as possible. It can be very helpful to tell the AI what you want your end result to be, so that it doesn’t do too much. For example: “We are going to create a PowerPoint presentation with no more than five slides”. Additionally, AI can be very chatty. You might ask the AI what the weather forecast is today, only to have it respond with the forecast, plus the long-range forecast, plus the latest trends, plus a comment about the prevailing winds. You can keep the AI’s responses to a minimum with commands like this: “Explain the difference between these two tools in one paragraph or less”, or “Explain the concept of function overloading in one sentence”. This makes the AI’s responses faster to read and less expensive. Rule #4: Put limits on the AI Last July, AI made the news when several OpenAI agents worked together to breach various systems, including a repository called Hugging Face. The story clearly illustrates what happens when appropriate guardrails are not put on AI. While less dramatic, you may find that your AI updates your code when you haven’t asked it to, or decides to write a Python script while executing a command because it would be more efficient. So it’s important to put limits on your AI when you give it tasks. Here are some examples of commands you might use: “Do NOT make any code changes without checking with me first”; “NEVER execute a POST call on this API; only GET calls”; “Do NOT look for authentication credentials if you lack them; ask me for the credentials instead”. Rule #5: Ask the right questions Your AI can be a fount of information if you ask it the right questions. Asking more specific questions will yield the best results. Instead of saying “Why is my automated test failing?”, you could ask “On what line is this test failing?” or “What credentials are used in this test?”, or “What environment is this test pointing to?”. title: 12 BEST AI Test Automation Tools for 2026 The Third Wave
text: The Bottom Line for 2026: The best AI test automation tools for 2026, by category: agentic testing with no script (Thunders.ai, QA.tech, Perfecto), autonomous test creation (mabl, testers.ai), visual AI (Applitools), all-in-one and codeless platforms (Katalon, ACCELQ, TestMu KaneAI), open source AI on the framework you already use (Alumnium), AI-authored mobile tests (Maestro), and AI failure analysis inside your pipeline (Testkube). I’ve spent 25+ years in QA and interviewed 600+ automation experts on the TestGuild podcast, and most “AI testing tools” are still GPT wrappers. The 12 below are the ones I’ve used, demoed, or grilled the founders on, and they’re the ones I’d actually shortlist. If you want a shortlist for your specific stack, use my free Tool Matcher. Otherwise, here are the 12 AI testing tools worth your time. Why you can trust this list: Every tool here is one I’ve covered on TestGuild with the people who actually build it or use it. The quotes you’ll read come straight from those podcast interviews. They’re real conversations, not AI-generated summaries. Many of these companies also sponsor TestGuild, and every one of them is tagged “TestGuild sponsor” right under its name. Sponsorship buys access to my audience, not a spot on this list. Some sponsors aren’t on it, and at least one tool that has never paid me is. AI Testing Waves I first wrote about the AI “three waves” back in 2017, and honestly? I thought I was just documenting a trend. Turns out, I was watching a revolution. (Quick note: I first wrote this in 2017, updated it in 2023, and I’m updating it again now in 2026. Two tools that were on this list are gone, which tells you something about how fast this is moving.) Here’s what’s wild: back in 2017, when I first started talking about AI in testing on my TestGuild podcast, people thought I was overselling it. “Joe, is this just hype?” they’d ask. In our State of Automation 2027 survey, only 6.4% of the 485 testers who answered said their team isn’t using AI in testing at all. 40.8% said it’s already standard practice across their teams. The question isn’t “should we use AI?” anymore. It’s “which AI tool won’t waste our time?” AI test manager testers.ai (CARBON) Open source, runs in your coding agent Agentic workflows Mabl Autonomous test agents QA agents in your workflow Amikoo Agents test every PR and Jira story Visual testing Applitools Visual AI pioneer Codeless automation ACCELQ Generative AI test creation AI failure analysis Testkube AI root cause analysis in your own cluster Agentic, no script Perfecto Goal-based tests across web and mobile LLM-powered TestMu KaneAI Natural language tests Open source AI Alumnium AI layer on Selenium, Playwright, Appium Plain-English agents Thunders.ai Tests written in business language PR verification QA.tech Agents verify every pull request Mobile AI Maestro AI-authored, deterministic mobile tests Find the Right Test Tool For You Now with our Tool Matcher Frequently Asked Questions About AI Test Automation Tools Will AI test automation replace QA engineers? No, and I’ll tell you why after interviewing 600+ testing leaders on TestGuild Podcast, AI handles the grunt work that burns out good engineers. We’re talking test generation, flake detection, self-healing selectors, the repetitive stuff that makes testers want to quit. But here’s what AI can’t do: understand business risk, know which bugs actually matter to users, or make judgment calls when your test results are ambiguous. The teams I’ve talked to at Automation Guild who are winning with AI? They’re using it to amplify their engineers’ impact, not replace them. Test everything and keep the good, including the human expertise. Are AI test automation tools ready for real production use? Some are, most aren’t.
